newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Brazil to cut jobs, even if reform fails.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brazil to cut jobs, even if reform fails.

text.p: Brazil's government may be forced to take "drastic" steps to cut jobs if it loses a crucial, upcoming vote on its civil service reform bill, Claudia Costin, the Administration Ministry's executive secretary, said.
"If (the reform) is significantly changed, the government will not bother to keep it...and could adopt extreme measures," Costin said in an interview with Reuters.

The reform bill, which has been stuck in Congress for more than two years, faces a make-or-break vote when an opposition amendment aimed at stopping mass dismissals of civil servants is put to the Chamber of Deputies, probably in August.

The amendment would strip the bill of a central article that allows federal, state and municipal authorities that spend more than 60 percent of their receipts on payrolls to fire workers, including those with job guarantees.
The article represents much of the bite of the civil service reform which, if fully approved, would produce savings equivalent to 0.78 percent of Brazil's gross domestic product, Costin said.
Without the article, however, the bill would be effectively useless.

"Cities and states will be condemned to having no real government," said Costin. "(The 60 percent rule) is fundamental because the situation we're in is unsustainable, not just from the fiscal point of view, but also in terms of governability."
Brazilian states spend on average 74 percent of their receipts on payrolls. Some spend more than 100 percent, at the expense of their crumbling social services.

Teachers, health workers and police officers have taken to the streets recently over their tiny salaries. Governors say they cannot offer any more because they have to spend so much on unproductive, unfireable administrative workers.

Despite the urgency of the problem, however, many government-allied members of the Chamber of Deputies are expected to back the opposition over its amendment for fear of losing voters or their powerful public sector backers.
In Brazil's more remote regions, public jobs are the mainstay of economies. In Roraima state, near Venezuela, federal employees represent 80 percent of the adult workforce.

Nor can lawmakers hide from the civil service lobby in the purpose-built, administrative capital Brasilia, the only place in Brazil where where local businessmen fear the effect of a cutback on public spending.

Earlier this month, the government mustered just one vote more than the minimum 308 needed to kill another opposition amendment which would have prevented federal and local authorities from sacking incompetent workers.

Costin, whose family has received death threats for her role in the reform drive, predicted the upcoming amendment vote would be just as close. "These are not banal issues. Brazil's political culture is not used to change like this," she said.

If the opposition amendment was approved, preventing the mass sacking of workers, then the government would abandon its attempts to get the troublesome reform through Congress and take other "drastic" measures to cut costs, she said.
Those measures might include the dismissal of up to 55,000 federal workers, or ten percent of the total workforce, who do not qualify for job protection and could be fired via presidential decree.
The government could also force state governments to adopt similarly tough measures by linking payroll cuts to improved terms in ongoing debt renegotiations, Costin said.

Further cuts might be made if the government stuck to the letter of a law approved in 1995, which would prevent state governments from awarding any pay rises after 1998 if their payroll spending remains above 60 percent of receipts.
"These would be much more traumatic moves," said Costin.
By sidestepping Congress to implement sweeping job cuts, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso would expose himself to a wave of criticism just as he seeks re-election next year.
